title: 📘 UNIT 6: AFRICA AND THE OUTSIDE WORLD: 1500–1880s
notes:
This unit focuses on Africa's relationships with the outside world from the 16th to the 19th centuries and how these relationships contributed to European conquest and colonization.

🌍 Major themes → medieval African states + European contacts + Portuguese expansion + slave trade + legitimate trade + white settlement in South Africa + European explorers and missionaries.

📌 The period ended with increasing European competition for African territory, leading toward the Scramble and Partition of Africa in the 1880s.

title: 6.1 👑 Medieval African States
notes:
The 16th–19th centuries were characterized by state formation, expansion of long-distance trade and the spread of Islam.

Major regions and states →

• Northeast/Northern Africa → Funj Sultanate + Morocco + Ottoman North Africa.

• West Africa → Benin + Oyo + Dahomey + Ashante + Sokoto Caliphate.

• East Africa → Buganda + Rwanda.

• West-Central Africa → Kongo.

• South-Central Africa → Torwa + Mwene Mutapa + Rozwi.

• Southern Africa → Zulu Kingdom.

📌 Agriculture, cattle, handicrafts, trade, warfare and religion contributed to the rise and development of African states.

title: 6.1.1 🕌 Funj Sultanate
notes:
1275 → Nubian Christian kingdoms of Alwa and Makuria were annexed by the Egyptian Mamluks.

14th century → Arab clans and Islam expanded into Nubia.

Funj → cattle-keeping pastoral people who challenged Arab supremacy.

1504 → Funj Sultanate established at Sennar.

👤 Amara Dunqas → important Funj leader who fought the Abdallabi state for supremacy.

Major features → territorial expansion + Islamization + Arab-Nubian intermarriage + cultural Africanization.

1620 → King Susenyos attacked the Funj.
1742 & 1744 → King Iyasu II launched two expeditions; the second ended in a major Funj-Arab victory.

Funj later extended influence over Kordofan and Darfur.

1821 → conquered by Muhammad Ali's Egypt.

title: 6.1.1 🇲🇦 Rise of the Moroccan Sultanate
notes:
16th century → Morocco emerged as an independent North African state.

👑 Ahmad al-Mansur (1578–1603) → Morocco reached its height of power.

1578 → Morocco defeated and expelled the Portuguese from the North African coast.

1591 → Moroccan army crossed the Sahara and attacked the Songhay Empire to control its gold resources.

📍 Gao & Timbuktu → captured and looted by Moroccan forces.

Consequences → Songhay Empire disintegrated + Timbuktu's culture was damaged + gold trade routes shifted.

1603 → death of Ahmad al-Mansur caused dynastic struggles and division between Fez and Marrakesh.

1669 → Alawid Dynasty established and restored Moroccan unity.

Arma → Moroccan military forces and settlers who controlled parts of the Niger bend.

1737 → Arma rule collapsed after Tuareg Berbers gained control of Timbuktu and the Niger bend.

title: 6.1.2 🏛️ Benin, Oyo, Dahomey, Ashante & Sokoto
notes:
🏛️ BENIN
Edo people → established the Empire of Benin in southern Nigeria during the 14th–15th centuries.

Capital → Benin City.

Economy → agriculture + ocean trade.

Trade → pepper and dyed cotton goods exchanged for European manufactured products.
Famous achievement → bronze sculptures.
Decline → began in the 17th century.

⚔️ OYO
17th century → Yoruba chieftaincies united to form Oyo Empire.
Economy → mainly agriculture + spinning + dyeing + metalwork.
19th century → declined because of neighboring invasions and rebellions.

☪️ SOKOTO CALIPHATE
Fulani expanded into Hausa land after the decline of Oyo.

👤 Usman dan Fodio → Fulani Muslim cleric whose jihads helped establish the Sokoto Caliphate during the early 19th century.

🛡️ DAHOMEY

1625 → became an independent kingdom.

19th century → reached great power.

Major role → participated heavily in the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.

👩‍🦰 Abomey Amazons → elite female military regiments, about 2,000–6,000 soldiers.

👑 ASHANTE
Akan warrior state centered at Kumasi.

Economy → gold + tribute + trade + kola nuts.

Ashantehene → king of Ashante.

Late 17th century → united much of present-day Ghana.

18th century → expanded north to protect gold trade.

19th century → expanded toward the coast.

Government → officials increasingly appointed according to ability.

title: 6.1.3 🌍 Eastern African States
notes:
🌿 BUGANDA
Location → fertile region northwest of Lake Victoria.

👑 Kabaka → title of the king of Buganda.

18th century → Buganda expanded over a large area of present-day Uganda.

Economy → agriculture + trade + handicrafts.

🐄 RWANDA

Located southwest of Buganda.

Tutsi → ruling class.

Hutu → mainly agricultural population.

Economy and society → cattle keeping + farming + tribute collection.

📌 The Great Lakes region developed kingdoms through interaction between pastoral and agricultural communities.

title: 6.1.4 🏛️ Kongo, Torwa, Mwene Mutapa & Rozwi
notes:
🏛️ KINGDOM OF KONGO
Emergence → about 1400.

Location → south of Congo River, present-day DRC and northern Angola.
People → Bakongo.

👑 Manikongo → title of the king.

Capital → Mbanza Kongo.

Government → centralized; six provinces with appointed governors.

Economy → agriculture + regional/coastal trade.

Trade goods → iron tools + pottery + salt + textiles + ivory + slaves + copper.

Decline → Portuguese slave raiding + internal unrest + Jaga/Imbangala invasions.

🏰 TORWA
15th century → successor to Great Zimbabwe.

Capital → Khami/Danangombe.

Known for → advanced stone enclosure architecture and long-distance trade.

💰 MWENE MUTAPA
Founder → Mutota.

Successor → Matope.

Controlled → territory and long-distance trade between the plateau and Swahili coast.

Main resources → gold + ivory.

16th century → dominated Zambezi Valley trade.

Portuguese influence increased during the 16th–17th centuries.

⚔️ ROZWI
Founder/leader → Changamire.

1680s → conquered Torwa.

1693 → expelled Portuguese from Zimbabwe plateau.

1830 → Rozwi was destroyed by Nguni and Ndebele movements connected to the rise of the Zulu Empire.

title: 6.1.5 🛡️ The Zulu Kingdom
notes:
Southern Africa → home of Bantu-speaking peoples including Venda, Sotho, Tsongo, Nguni and Inhambane.

Major state formation → developed mainly during the late 18th and 19th centuries.

Causes → inter-group conflicts + population movements + Boer expansion + British colonization.

👑 Shaka Zulu (1818–1828) → transformed the Zulu Kingdom into a dominant regional power.
👩 Queen Nandi → supported Shaka during his rise.

Shaka → successfully defended the kingdom against neighboring Bantu groups and Boers.

After Shaka → internal wars and conflict with British colonizers weakened the kingdom.

1860s → British forces conquered the Zulu Kingdom and other Bantu states.

title: 6.1.6 🇹🇷 Ottoman Conquest of North Africa
notes:
16th century → Ottoman Empire and Spain competed for control of North Africa.

1517 → Ottomans conquered Egypt by defeating the Mamluks.

Ottoman control → Libya + Algeria + Tunisia + parts of Nubia; Morocco remained outside Ottoman rule.

Ottoman military strength → navy + Janissaries + provincial cavalry known as spahis.

Administration → provinces → Sanjaks → districts.

👤 Pasha → provincial governor.
👤 Dey → military commander/ruler in some provinces.
👤 Bey → hereditary/local ruler in areas such as Egypt and Tunisia.

18th century → many North African rulers became practically independent while recognizing Ottoman suzerainty.

1805 → Muhammad Ali established a new ruling dynasty in Egypt.

1830s–1840s → France occupied Algeria.

📌 Ottoman rule was often nominal rather than direct, especially from the 18th century.

title: 6.2 🌍 Contacts of Africa with the Outside World
notes:
European contact with much of Africa increased from the 15th century.

🇵🇹 Portugal → first European power to establish extensive contacts along African coasts.

Main motives →
• Direct access to West African gold.
• Bypass Arab middlemen.
• Avoid Turkish control/blockades of trade routes.
• Reach Asian/Far Eastern trade directly.
• Obtain valuable African resources.

👑 Henry the Navigator → supported Portuguese exploration.

📌 Early coastal contacts later developed into European commercial, military and colonial expansion.

title: 6.2.1 🚢 Portuguese Contacts with Africa
notes:
1415 → Portugal occupied Ceuta in Morocco.
1418 → reached Madeira and established a colony at Porto Santo.
1430–1490 → Portuguese sailors explored the western African coast from Morocco to the Cape of Good Hope.
1446 → established trading posts on the Senegal coast.

Atlantic islands → Madeira + Azores + Cape Verde became Portuguese bases and plantation centers.

Sugar plantations → worked largely with enslaved African labor.

1482 → Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo River.

🇦🇴 Ndongo → Portuguese alliance with the Ngola; the name Angola came from the title Ngola.

👑 Queen Nzinga Mbande (1581–1663) → powerful Ndongo leader, diplomat and military strategist who resisted Portuguese expansion for decades.

1656 → Nzinga signed a peace treaty with Portugal after prolonged conflict.

title: 6.2.2 ⛵ Portuguese Expansion in Kongo & East Africa
notes:
1482 → Kongo established an alliance with Portugal.
1489 → Kongolese embassy sent to Portugal.
1491 → Portuguese missionaries and craftsmen entered Kongo.

👑 Afonso I (1507–1542/43) → adopted Portuguese cultural and governmental influences and built churches.

Kongo later became a major supplier of enslaved Africans to the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.

1665 → Portuguese forces invaded Kongo, killed the Manikongo and ended its independence.

1497–1498 → Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape and reached Swahili ports including Malindi and Mombasa before continuing to India.

Portuguese actions → captured Swahili trading cities + damaged their trade and culture + established military/trading posts along Mozambique.

1573 → Portuguese gained mining and settlement privileges in Mwene Mutapa.
1628–29 → Portuguese defeated the ruler's forces and increased control.
1693 → Changamire and the Rozwi expelled the Portuguese from the region.

📌 By the late 17th century, Omani Arabs also expelled Portuguese forces from East African ports north of Mozambique.

title: 6.3 ⛓️ Slavery and Slave Trade in Africa
notes:
Slavery existed in African societies before the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.

Enslavement methods → warfare + raiding + kidnapping + tribute + market supply + pawning.

Slaves were used in:
• Domestic service.
• Agriculture and animal rearing.
• Hunting and fishing.
• Mining.
• Salt production.
• Ironworking.
• Weaving and crafts.
• Trade and transport.
• Military service.
• Palace administration.

📌 In some societies slaves could marry free people, own/farm land, inherit property, gain social mobility or obtain manumission.

⚠️ Treatment varied greatly by society, owner and historical period.

title: 6.3.1 🌊 Indian Ocean & Mediterranean Slave Trade
notes:
African slaves were exported outside Africa long before the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.

🏜️ Trans-Saharan trade → connected Mediterranean/North Africa with sub-Saharan Africa.
Main participants → Arab and Berber merchants.
Trade → slaves + gold + salt and other commodities.

🔴 Red Sea trade → slaves from the Ethiopian region and Nubia were transported toward the Middle East and India.

🌊 Indian Ocean trade → slaves from East Africa were transported to Arabia, the Persian Gulf, India and Indian Ocean plantations.

18th century → Indian Ocean slave trade expanded strongly.

1770s → French sugar and coffee plantations in Mauritius and Réunion increased demand for East African slaves.

19th century → Zanzibar became an important center of the East African slave trade, with Omani Arab influence extending along the coast.

title: 6.3.2 🔺 Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
notes:
1492 → Columbus's voyage to America contributed to the expansion of European plantations and mining in the Americas.

Amerindian populations → suffered greatly from European diseases, violence and exploitation, creating a severe labor shortage.

Europeans increasingly turned to Africa for plantation labor.

🇵🇹 Portugal → first European country to transport African slaves across the Atlantic.
1532 → African captives were directly transported across the Atlantic.

After the 1630s → Dutch, French, British and Danish involvement increased.
18th century → Britain became the largest exporter of African slaves.

Major sources → West and Central African coastal regions, including Kongo and the Slave Coast.

📌 The trade lasted from the 16th to the mid-19th century.

title: 6.3.3 🔺 The Triangular Trade
notes:
The triangular trade connected three continents → Europe + Africa + Americas.

1️⃣ EUROPE → AFRICA
European merchants brought → clothes + alcohol + metal goods + firearms.

⬇️ exchanged for

2️⃣ AFRICA → AMERICAS
African captives were transported across the Atlantic.

⬇️ exchanged for

3️⃣ AMERICAS → EUROPE
Plantation products → sugar + tobacco + rum + other commodities.

These products were transported to Europe and sold for profit.

💰 Result → enormous European wealth accumulation and increased capital that contributed to Western Europe's industrial development.

title: 6.3.4 🚢 Phases of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
notes:
1️⃣ PIRATIC SLAVE TRADE
15th century–late 16th century.
Individual merchants, adventurers and sea raiders dominated.
European governments had little direct involvement.
Slave trade volume was relatively low because gold was still a major priority.

2️⃣ MONOPOLISTIC SLAVE TRADE
1580s–second half of the 17th century.
Chartered European companies controlled the trade with government support and armed forces.
Major sources → Kongo + Slave Coast.

💰 Enslaved people bought cheaply in Africa and sold at much higher prices in the Americas.

3️⃣ FREE TRADE
Second half of the 17th century onward.
Individual traders increasingly participated.
1689 → Britain permitted individuals in the empire to participate in commercial activities including slave trading.
Competition among companies and individual merchants increased.

title: 6.3.5 ⛓️ Middle Passage & Resistance
notes:
Middle Passage → forced Atlantic voyage carrying enslaved Africans from Africa to the Americas.

Conditions →
• Captives chained together.
• Severe overcrowding and poor sanitation.
• Hunger, disease and violence.
• Many died during the journey.

📌 About one-sixth of captives may have died during the Atlantic crossing.

Plantation life → extremely harsh labor from dawn to dusk, often under chains and brutal conditions.

✊ Resistance → Africans resisted through revolts during capture, the Middle Passage and plantation life.

📌 Resistance was often violently suppressed.

title: 6.3.6 🕊️ Abolition of the Slave Trade
notes:
Abolitionist pressure increased during the late 18th century.

Main influences →
• Humanitarian opposition.
• Religious movements.
• Enlightenment ideas.
• French Revolution ideals.
• Growing criticism of brutality and immorality.
• Economic changes caused by industrialization.

📅 Major abolition dates:
1803 → Denmark.
1807 → Britain.
1808 → United States.
1813 → Sweden.
1814 → Netherlands.
1818 → France.

🇬🇧 Britain → used its navy to enforce anti-slave-trade laws.

Industrial Revolution → shifted European economic interests toward raw materials, cheap labor and markets rather than slave trading.

📌 Abolition of the Atlantic trade did not immediately end slavery in Africa or other slave-trading systems.

title: 6.3.7 📉 Effects of the Slave Trade on Africa
notes:
Nearly 18 million enslaved people were shipped through the major African slave trades between 1500 and 1900; about 12 million were associated with the Trans-Atlantic trade.

Negative effects →
• Loss of millions of people.
• Destruction of some communities.
• Family separation and population displacement.
• Political instability.
• Warfare and insecurity.
• Decline of agricultural production.
• Drain of productive manpower.
• Economic disruption.
• Delayed development of productive forces.

⚠️ Some states such as Dahomey, Ashante and Oyo gained wealth and political strength from participation in the trade.

📌 The slave trade therefore produced both short-term gains for some rulers and merchants and severe long-term demographic, political and economic damage across many African societies.

title: 6.4 💱 The Legitimate Trade
notes:
After European governments increasingly outlawed the Atlantic slave trade, European merchants promoted what they called the 'Legitimate Trade'.

19th century exports replaced slaves with African commodities.

Major exports →
• Gum Arabic → mainly Senegal.
• Groundnuts → Guinea.
• Palm oil → coastal forest regions of West Africa.

🌴 Palm oil → became West Africa's major overseas export by the mid-19th century and was important as a lubricant for European industrial machinery before petroleum became dominant.

African rulers and merchants organized production, sometimes using internal slave labor.

⚠️ Problems → benefits were concentrated among wealthy rulers and merchants + European imports did little to strengthen indigenous economies + European traders increasingly sought control over African internal trade.

📌 Intensifying European commercial competition contributed to the Scramble for Africa in the 1870s–1880s.

title: 6.5 🇿🇦 White Settlement in South Africa
notes:
1652 → Dutch East India Company established a permanent settlement at the Cape of Good Hope.

Initial purposes → supply passing ships with fresh food + support sick sailors + protect the settlement and trade.

1657 → some company soldiers became permanent farmers called Boers (later Afrikaners).

Boer expansion → conflict with Khoisan communities over grazing land and cattle.

1659 → First Khoi-Dutch War.
1673–1677 → Second Khoisan-Dutch War.

European settlement expanded while Khoisan communities were weakened by warfare and disease.

18th century → Boers expanded eastward toward Zulu and Xhosa territories.

1795 → Britain took control of the Cape Colony.

1830s–1840s → Boers moved north across the Vaal and Orange Rivers in the Great Trek.

Four Boer colonies → Cape + Natal + Transvaal + Orange Free State.

1860s → discovery of mineral deposits attracted many European settlers.

📌 By the end of the 19th century → Britain controlled all four major South African colonies.

title: 6.5.1 ⚔️ Conflicts in South Africa
notes:
Main causes of conflict →
• Expansion of Boer settlement.
• Competition for land and grazing areas.
• Cattle raiding.
• British expansion.
• Economic and mineral interests.
• Expansion of African kingdoms such as the Zulu.

Khoisan peoples → lost large areas of land and suffered from warfare and smallpox.

Bantu-speaking peoples → were increasingly pushed from fertile lands toward less favorable areas.

📌 Indigenous populations increasingly became sources of cheap labor for the settler economy.

title: 6.6 🧭 European Explorers & Missionaries: 1770–1870
notes:
European exploration increased as Europeans sought information about Africa's resources, trade routes, rivers, labor and markets.

1788 → African Association formed by wealthy Englishmen.
Main aims → explore Timbuktu + investigate the Niger River.

Main explorers →
👤 Richard Burton.
👤 John Hanning Speke.
👤 James Grant.
👤 David Livingstone.
👤 Henry Morton Stanley.

Exploration became important in opening the interior of Africa to European commercial and political expansion.

title: 6.6.1 🗺️ Major European Explorers
notes:
👤 Richard Burton + John Hanning Speke + James Grant
1850s–1860s → investigated the White Nile and Lake Victoria region and demonstrated the river's navigable possibilities upstream from Khartoum.

👤 David Livingstone
Explored → Zambezi River + Shire River + Lake Malawi and other South-Central African river/lake systems.

👤 Henry Morton Stanley
1876 → sailed down the Zaire/Congo River from an upper tributary.

📌 Stanley demonstrated the navigability of the Congo River.

👑 Leopold II of Belgium → became highly interested in Stanley's exploration and sent him back to the Congo basin in 1879.

⚠️ European exploration helped prepare the way for later colonial control.

title: 6.6.2 💰 Motives Behind European Exploration
notes:
European exploration was driven by:
• Search for raw materials.
• Search for cheap labor.
• Search for new markets.
• Desire to control African natural wealth.
• Interest in trade routes.
• Desire to discover navigable rivers.
• Expansion of European political influence.

🌊 Major rivers investigated → Upper Nile + Zambezi + Zaire/Congo.

📌 Rivers were viewed as natural 'highways' connecting European traders with Africa's interior.

💊 Malaria → major obstacle to European exploration because of high European mortality.

1850s → discovery/use of quinine provided greater protection against malaria and accelerated European exploration.

title: 6.6.3 ✝️ European Missionaries in Africa
notes:
19th century → European Christian missionary activity expanded in Africa.

Major missionary organizations →
• Anglican Church Missionary Society (CMS).
• Wesleyan Methodist/London Missionary Society (LMS).
• Moravian missionaries.
• Protestant missionaries from France, Germany, Holland and the United States.
• French Catholic missions later expanded.

Successful early areas → Sierra Leone + Liberia + Southern Africa.

Missionaries often worked among → freed slaves + poor communities + Khoisan + mixed-race populations.

Missionary attractions → education + literacy + technical skills + access to European knowledge and firearms.

📌 Mission stations were initially concentrated mainly in coastal areas.

title: 6.6.4 ⚠️ Missionaries & Colonialism
notes:
Missionary progress in much of Africa was slow during the early and mid-19th century.

By the 1880s → Christian converts were still less than 1% of non-Muslim Africans, excluding Ethiopia.

Because of limited progress, some missionaries appealed to European governments for intervention.

📌 European explorers provided geographical and economic information.
📌 Missionaries established cultural and social contacts.
📌 Together, these activities helped open African societies to greater European intervention.

⚠️ In the final quarter of the 19th century, missionary activities sometimes contributed to the development and justification of European colonial expansion.

title: 🏆 UNIT 6 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
👑 MEDIEVAL AFRICAN STATES

Funj → Sennar → 1504 → Islamization → conquered by Egypt in 1821.

Morocco → Ahmad al-Mansur → 1591 attack on Songhay → Alawid Dynasty 1669.

Benin → Edo → Benin City → bronze art → ocean trade.

Oyo → Yoruba → agriculture + crafts → declined in 19th century.

Dahomey → 1625 → slave trade → Abomey Amazons.

Ashante → Kumasi → gold + tribute + trade.

Sokoto → Usman dan Fodio → Fulani jihad.

Buganda → Kabaka → Lake Victoria region.

Rwanda → Tutsi ruling class + Hutu agricultural population.

Kongo → Manikongo → Mbanza Kongo → centralized government.

Mwene Mutapa → Mutota → gold + ivory → Zambezi trade.

Rozwi → Changamire → expelled Portuguese in 1693.

Zulu → Shaka Zulu → regional dominance.

🇵🇹 EUROPEAN CONTACTS

Portugal → first major European power to explore African coasts.

Henry the Navigator → supported exploration.

Diogo Cão → Congo River, 1482.

Vasco da Gama → Swahili coast → India, 1497–98.

Queen Nzinga → resistance against Portuguese expansion.

⛓️ SLAVE TRADE

Indigenous slavery → existed before Atlantic trade.

Trans-Saharan → Sahara → North Africa/Mediterranean.

Red Sea → Ethiopian region/Nubia → Middle East/India.

Indian Ocean → East Africa → Arabia/India/plantations.

Trans-Atlantic → Africa → Americas.

🔺 TRIANGULAR TRADE

Europe → manufactured goods/firearms → Africa.

Africa → enslaved people → Americas.

Americas → sugar/tobacco/rum → Europe.

🕊️ ABOLITION

1803 → Denmark.

1807 → Britain.

1808 → United States.

1813 → Sweden.

1814 → Netherlands.

1818 → France.

💱 LEGITIMATE TRADE

Gum Arabic + groundnuts + palm oil replaced slave exports.

Palm oil → major West African export.

European competition → contributed to Scramble for Africa.

🇿🇦 SOUTH AFRICA

1652 → Dutch Cape settlement.

1657 → Boers settled as farmers.

1659 → First Khoi-Dutch War.

1795 → Britain took Cape Colony.

1830s–1840s → Great Trek.

1860s → mineral discoveries attracted settlers.

🧭 EXPLORERS
Burton + Speke + Grant → White Nile/Lake Victoria.

Livingstone → Zambezi + Lake Malawi region.

Stanley → Congo/Zaire River.

✝️ MISSIONARIES

CMS + LMS + Moravian + Protestant + Catholic missions.

Main motives/roles → Christianity + education + literacy + cultural contact.


🧠 EXAM CONNECTION:
Trade + Islam → strengthened many African states.
European exploration → opened African interior to European economic and political interests.

Slave trade → caused major demographic, political and economic disruption.

Legitimate trade → replaced slave exports with African commodities but increased European economic control.

Exploration + missionary activity → helped prepare the way for colonial expansion.
